questions.q: What does successfully driving the loss to near-zero on a single overfit batch confirm?
options: That the model will generalize well to the full dataset
That gradients are flowing and the model/loss/optimizer wiring is correct, which is a prerequisite before trusting any larger result
That the learning rate is already optimally tuned
That the model has no numerical precision issues under mixed precision
questions.explain: The overfit-a-batch check only verifies the pipeline's wiring is correct — it says nothing about generalization, but a failure here means something is broken before any larger run is worth trusting.

questions.q: Why can a parameter with a dead (missing or all-zero) gradient sometimes go unnoticed even when the overfit-a-batch check passes?
options: Because dead gradients always cause the loss to become NaN immediately
Because the rest of the model may still be able to drive the loss down without that parameter's contribution, masking the fact that one parameter never updates
Because PyTorch automatically removes parameters with dead gradients
Because the overfit check only runs for parameters with requires_grad=False
questions.explain: If other parameters can compensate, the overall loss can still decrease even though one specific parameter never receives a usable gradient — which is why a dedicated per-parameter gradient audit is a separate, necessary check.

questions.q: What does the input-ablation check (feeding random noise instead of real input) test for?
options: Whether the model is overfitting to the training data
Whether the model is actually using the real input in a meaningful way — if noise scores about the same as real input, the data likely isn't reaching the model correctly
Whether the optimizer's learning rate is too high
Whether the model's gradients are numerically stable
questions.explain: A model that depends on its input should perform meaningfully worse on random noise than on real input. If the loss barely changes, it suggests the data pipeline or model isn't actually using the input as intended.

questions.q: What does it mean if a sophisticated model's score is close to or worse than a trivial baseline like 'predict the mean'?
options: The model is performing exceptionally well and the baseline is irrelevant
Something is likely wrong with the implementation, since the model isn't learning anything beyond what the trivial baseline already captures
The baseline must be miscalculated, since models always beat trivial baselines
The model needs more training epochs to eventually separate from the baseline
questions.explain: A sophisticated model should meaningfully outperform a trivial baseline. Scoring at or near that baseline is a strong signal of a bug, before even considering whether the architecture itself is a good choice.

questions.q: According to the lesson, why should this sanity-check checklist be run on every new experiment, not just once when a codebase is first built?
options: Because the checks become invalid after the first run and must be redone for compliance reasons
Because a new architecture variant, loss term, or data pipeline change can reintroduce exactly the bugs these checks catch, even in a codebase that passed them before
Because GPUs degrade over time and need to be re-verified
Because the checks are only valid for exactly 24 hours after being run
questions.explain: Each check is cheap, and new changes to the architecture, loss, or data pipeline can reintroduce the same categories of bugs. Treating the checklist as a one-time rite of passage misses bugs introduced by later changes.
